newsitem.title: GERMANY: German grain trade eyes harvest at Hamburg meeting.
newsitem.headline: German grain trade eyes harvest at Hamburg meeting.

text.p: Cereals harvests in northern Germany were still underway as traders on Tuesday held informal marketing discussions scheduled earlier in the year.

"Harvests are delayed this year but wheat yields and volumes are looking good in the north," said Peter Viezens, the general secretary of the grain and feeds trade association, which is hosting the Tuesday meeting attended by more than 400 northern European traders.
"Rye ergot levels are low and even if falling numbers should disqualify rye for bread flour -- the markets have learnt to live with additional feedgrain supplies."

The export-intensive farm regions of Lower Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg, which together account for some 12 million out of Germany's 40 million tonne crop, show relatively better wheat and rye quality than others.
They share with other regions a sharp decline in barley and rapeseed yields after a harsh winter which also hit wheat protein contents and Hagbergs, which indicate baking quality.
But they suffered less damage to rye from rain during harvesting. This has affected quality in many other areas.
A grain broker said the prospects of a high German crop volume, due to area expansions, with some quality problems should make markets more inward-looking this year.
"We're currently out of export markets because we're 10-20 marks a tonne above the rest of Europe," he said.
"There is a lot of talk about crop pressure from other EU countries but it has not affected domestic prices that much."
"There are also wheat inquiries from Poland where we have a logistics advantage via rail across the border."
A trader with an international grain house confirmed the view of German price stability amid latent domestic demand.
"Even if slightly lower qualities don't make German grain an export hit this year, there is also the chance of delivering into grain intervention," he said.
"Consumers may be taking a relaxed attitude now, but storeholders are hungry for grain and may pay premiums over the minimum buying-in price."
"This means farmers don't need to rush into post-harvest sales and the market will be given a firm price floor."
Germany's public grain stocks in July were only around 2.50 million tonnes versus 4.50 million a year earlier as the EU depleted stocks amid tight supply and global price rallies.
Fob Baltic wheat this week remained tradeless but nominal prices rose 2.50-5.00 marks a tonne to 280-310 marks.
Feeds brokers at the meeting said their customers in the compound feed industry were eagerly awaiting cheap feedgrain supplies for the autumn and winter months.
These should compete with imported meals, especially the U.S. soycomplex where prices are rising amid weather concern.
"Feed mixers have put buying on hold since July because they can't achieve good prices for their products," one said.
"Imported feeds have suffered most from this lull, which was worsened by the upheaval caused by the madcow crisis."
Oilseeds brokers said disappointing rapeseed crop progress had failed to boost domestic prices effectively.
"Crushers are ignoring the crop problems as they can't sell any oil, and meal alone cannot support crushings," said one.
"It's bad for producers -- prices of 450 marks free mill are down 40 marks from 1996 highs."
